t: Count Number of Distinct Integers After Reverse Operations
o: Append the digit-reversal of every original number, then count distinct values overall. Reversal drops leading zeros (10 → 1). Just put originals and reversals into a hash set and return its size. Example 1 gives {1,13,10,12,31} ∪ {1,31,1,21,13} = 6 distinct values. With n ≤ 1e5 and values ≤ 1e6, hashing is trivially efficient; arithmetic reversal avoids string overhead.
k: Set semantics: duplicates between originals and reversals collapse automatically.
Reverse arithmetically (while loop, ×10 + digit) to avoid string allocation.
Answer = size of set containing both nums and their reverses.

a.n: Approach 1: String Reversal into a Set
a.i: Convert to string, reverse, parse back, insert both values into a set.
s: Insert each num into the set.
a.t: O(n · d) where d ≤ 7 digits per number

a.i: Identical idea, but reversal via digit arithmetic avoids string conversions — marginally faster in practice.
s: For each num, compute reverse by repeated mod/divide.
Add both to a hash set.
a.t: O(n · d), d = number of digits ≤ 7

w: Both approaches are effectively equivalent; mention the string version for readability and the arithmetic one for speed. Pitfalls: trailing zeros (10 → 01 → 1) are handled naturally by arithmetic reversal. Follow-up: count distinct after repeatedly reversing the whole array k times, or do it without extra space (sort-based dedup).
